Which of the curves above is simple, closed, and negatively oriented?
questions.worked_solution:
A simple closed curve is positively oriented if, when traveling along it, one always has the curve interior to the left and the curve exterior to the right. Otherwise, the curve is negatively oriented. 

A curve is positively oriented if it is traversed counterclockwise and is negatively oriented if it is traversed clockwise.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the curves:

- Curve I is simple, closed, negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed clockwise.

- Curve II is simple, closed, negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed clockwise.

- Curve III is not simple.

- Curve IV is a simple and closed curve but it is not negatively oriented. The arrows indicate that the curve is traversed counterclockwise, so it is positively oriented.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
The level curves of the function $f(x,y)=9x+3y-4$ are given by $f(x,y)=c.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $c=0$ gives an ellipse

II. $c=-4$ gives a line

III. $c=5$ gives a hyperbola
questions.worked_solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}9x+3y-4 & =c \\ 3y & =-9x+c+4 \\ y & =-3x+\frac{c+4}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=0$ then the level curve is $y=-3x+\frac{4}{9},$ which is not an ellipse.

- If $c=-4$ then the level curve is $y=-3x,$ which is a line.

- If $c=5$ then the level curve is $y=-3x+3,$ which is not a hyperbola.

So, only statement II is true.

questions.problem: Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ What are the coordinates of $x$ relative to the basis $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\},$ where ${c}_{1}=3{b}_{2}$ and ${c}_{2}={b}_{1}+6{b}_{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{c}_{1}=3{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2}={b}_{1}+6{b}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we express the $b$'s in terms of $c$'s. From the first equation, we get 

$$
{b}_{2}=\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
{c}_{2}={b}_{1}+6(\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1})\,⟹\,{b}_{1}={c}_{2}-2{c}_{1}.
$$

Since $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$, we can write the vector $x$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =-5{b}_{1}+2{b}_{2} \\  & =-5({c}_{2}-2{c}_{1})+2(\frac{1}{3}{c}_{1}) \\  & =-5{c}_{2}+10{c}_{1}+\frac{2}{3}{c}_{1} \\  & =\frac{32}{3}{c}_{1}-5{c}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $[x]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{32}{3} \\ -5\end{aligned}].$

questions.problem:
Compute $P(-1<X<1)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{28}({x}^{2}+1),\, & -2\le x\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a<X<b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1<X<1) & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}\frac{3}{28}({x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{28}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{x}^{2}+1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{28}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{28}([\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}+(1)]-[\frac{1}{3}(-1)^{3}+(-1)]) \\  & =\frac{3}{28}([\frac{1}{3}+1]-[-\frac{1}{3}-1]) \\  & =\frac{3}{28}\cdot \frac{8}{3} \\  & =\frac{2}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $y=y(x)$ satisfies the equation ${y}^{″}+6{y}^{′}+8y=0,$ which of the following **cannot** be $y(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Assuming $y={e}^{\lambda x}$ and differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {e}^{\lambda x},\,{y}^{″}={\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}.
$$

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}{e}^{\lambda x}+6\lambda {e}^{\lambda x}+8{e}^{\lambda x} & =0 \\ {e}^{\lambda x}({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The auxiliary equation is therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Factoring the auxiliary equation results in

$$
(\lambda +2)(\lambda +4)=0,
$$

and so the solutions of the auxiliary equation  are $\lambda =-2$ or $\lambda =-4.$

Therefore, any linear combination of the functions ${e}^{-2x}$ and ${e}^{-4x}$ is a solution to the original differential equation. 

Among the given options, only ${e}^{-6x}$ is not a solution.

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=(2x+3y-4z)^{2}\,i+(2x+3y-4z)^{2}\,j+(2x+3y-4z)^{2}\,k.$ 
Find $∇\cdot F.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
∇\cdot F=\text{div}\,F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((2x+3y-4z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((2x+3y-4z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((2x+3y-4z)^{2}) \\  & =4(2x+3y-4z)+6(2x+3y-4z)-8(2x+3y-4z) \\  & =2(2x+3y-4z) \\  & =4x+6y-8z.\end{aligned}
$$

We start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to basis vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the reduced matrix has $3$ pivot columns (or alternatively, $3$ non-zero rows). 

Therefore, the dimension of the span is $3.$
